ONLY THEN: Make the claim\n\nSkip any step = lying, not verifying\n```\n\n## Product-Surface Verification\n\nWhen the work involves an app, UI, or product surface, verification must cover more than whether a single requested feature works.\n\nKeep verification proportional. STOP\n\n- Using \"should\", \"probably\", \"seems to\"\n- Expressing satisfaction before verification (\"Great!\", \"Perfect!\", \"Done!\", etc.)\n- About to commit/push/PR without verification\n- Trusting agent success reports\n- Accepting \"validated with mocks\" or \"placeholder works\" as completion\n- Relying on partial verification\n- Thinking \"just this once\"\n- Tired and wanting work over\n- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**\n\n## Rationalization Prevention\n\n| Excuse | Reality |\n|--------|---------|\n| \"Should work now\" | RUN the verification |\n| \"I'm confident\" | Confidence ≠ evidence |\n| \"Just this once\" | No exceptions |\n| \"Linter passed\" | Linter ≠ compiler |\n| \"Agent said success\" | Verify independently |\n| \"I'm tired\" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |\n| \"Partial check is enough\" | Partial proves nothing |\n| \"Different words so rule doesn't apply\" | Spirit over letter |\n\n## Key Patterns\n\n**Tests:**\n```\n✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] \"All tests pass\"\n❌ \"Should pass now\" / \"Looks correct\"\n```\n\n**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**\n```\n✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)\n❌ \"I've written a regression test\" (without red-green verification)\n```\n\n**Build:**\n```\n✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] \"Build passes\"\n❌ \"Linter passed\" (linter doesn't check compilation)\n```\n\n**Requirements:**\n```\n✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion\n❌ \"Tests pass, phase complete\"\n```\n\n**Agent delegation:**\n```\n✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state\n❌ Trust agent report\n```\n\n## Why This Matters\n\nFrom 24 failure memories:\n- your human partner said \"I don't believe you\" - trust broken\n- Undefined functions shipped - would crash\n- Missing requirements shipped - incomplete features\n- Time wasted on false completion → redirect → rework\n- Violates: \"Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced.\"\n\n## When To Apply\n\n**ALWAYS before:**\n- ANY variation of success/completion claims\n- ANY expression of satisfaction\n- ANY positive statement about work state\n- Committing, PR creation, task completion\n- Staging, committing, pushing, or opening a PR when the work could include secrets, local environment files, dependencies, caches, build outputs, logs, temporary files, or generated/intermediate artifacts\n- Moving to next task\n- Delegating to agents\n\nWhen a meaningful bug involved architecture, storage, memory, persistence, control planes, background workers, recovery, data loss, security, or a repeated wrong assumption, use `ultrapowers:learning-from-bugs` before claiming the fix is complete.\n\nWhen a React app has server state, optimistic UI, caches, polling, SSE/WebSocket streams, background jobs, or persisted runtime state, use `ultrapowers:client-server-state-invariants` to decide which race and synchronization tests are required before claiming completion.\n\nBefore any git publish step, verify `.gitignore` exists for the project and that `git status` does not include secrets, credentials, local environment files, `node_modules`, dependency caches, build outputs, coverage output, logs, temporary files, or intermediate/generated artifacts unless the human explicitly asked to version a specific generated artifact.\n\n**Rule applies to:**\n- Exact phrases\n- Paraphrases and synonyms\n- Implications of success\n- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness\n\n## The Bottom Line\n\n**No shortcuts for verification.**\n\nRun the command. Read the output. THEN claim the result.\n\nThis is non-negotiable.\n---\nname: learning-from-bugs\ndescription: Use when a meaningful bug, regression, architecture flaw, storage issue, memory problem, persistence failure, control-plane failure, or system-level failure has been diagnosed or fixed\n---\n\n# Learning From Bugs\n\nWhen a bug teaches something reusable, capture the lesson before moving on.\n\n## Use This For\n\nUse this after diagnosing or fixing bugs that involve:\n\n- architecture or ownership boundaries,\n- storage, persistence, migrations, caching, or file paths,\n- memory management, leaks, lifecycle, cleanup, or resource pressure,\n- concurrency, queues, retries, resumability, or recovery,\n- control planes, event streams, background workers, or long-running jobs,\n- security, data loss, user trust, or incident-like failures,\n- any bug that took repeated attempts or revealed a wrong mental model.\n\nSkip it for typos, obvious one-line UI mistakes, throwaway test fixture fixes, or purely local churn that will not help future work.\n\n## Required Output\n\nWrite a short learning note to:\n\n`docs/superpowers/learnings/YYYY-MM-DD-<bug-or-lesson-slug>.md`\n\nCreate the directory if needed.\n\nUse this shape:\n\n```markdown\n# [Lesson Title]\n\n**Date:** YYYY-MM-DD\n**Context:** [project, feature, or subsystem]\n**Symptom:** [what failed]\n**Root Cause:** [the real cause, not the symptom]\n**Fix:** [what changed]\n**Verification:** [commands, tests, or checks that proved it]\n**Prevention:** [what future agents should do differently]\n**Skill/Doc Updates:** [nearby skills or docs updated, or why no general update was needed]\n```\n\nKeep it concrete. Future agents should be able to read the note and avoid the same mistake.\n\n## Update The System When The Lesson Generalizes\n\nIf the bug reveals a reusable rule, update the nearest skill or defaults doc in the same change. That conflated informational usage telemetry with an explicit provider rejection.\n-**Fix:** Detect percentage-based usage progress notices and keep values below 100% out of quota recovery. Explicit exhaustion text and provider errors still enter the existing recovery path.\n-**Verification:** `pnpm exec vitest run tests/server/quota/reset-parser.test.ts` failed on the new 76% regression test before the parser change and passed afterward.\n+**Symptom:** A progress notice such as “You've used 76% of your weekly limit · resets Aug 3 at 8pm” was classified as a quota error and could park a run in `quota_waiting`. When Claude did explicitly reject a request with that reset date, the parser dropped “Aug 3” and scheduled the wake for Aug 2 at 8pm.\n+**Root Cause:** `looksLikeQuota` treated any text with reset language and a parseable reset time as exhaustion. That conflated informational usage telemetry with an explicit provider rejection. The time parser also recognized only the clock portion of a named month-and-day reset.\n+**Fix:** Detect percentage-based usage progress notices and keep values below 100% out of quota recovery. Explicit exhaustion text and provider errors still enter the existing recovery path. Named month-and-day reset times now retain their calendar date.\n+**Verification:** `pnpm exec vitest run tests/server/quota/reset-parser.test.ts` failed on the new 76% and named-date regression tests before their respective parser changes and passed afterward.\n*** End Patch";

Reset schedules and usage percentages are supporting metadata, not blocking signals by themselves.\n    10\t**Skill/Doc Updates:** No shared skill update was needed; this rule is specific to OmniHarness quota parsing and is covered by the regression test and this project note.\n"

Delete it. Start over.\n\n**No exceptions:**\n- Don't keep it as \"reference\"\n- Don't \"adapt\" it while writing tests\n- Don't look at it\n- Delete means delete\n\nImplement fresh from tests. Period.\n\n## Red-Green-Refactor\n\n```dot\ndigraph tdd_cycle {\n    rankdir=LR;\n    red [label=\"RED\\nWrite failing test\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ffcccc\"];\n    verify_red [label=\"Verify fails\\ncorrectly\", shape=diamond];\n    green [label=\"GREEN\\nMinimal code\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ccffcc\"];\n    verify_green [label=\"Verify passes\\nAll green\", shape=diamond];\n    refactor [label=\"REFACTOR\\nClean up\", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=\"#ccccff\"];\n    next [label=\"Next\", shape=ellipse];\n\n    red -> verify_red;\n    verify_red -> green [label=\"yes\"];\n    verify_red -> red [label=\"wrong\\nfailure\"];\n    green -> verify_green;\n    verify_green -> refactor [label=\"yes\"];\n    verify_green -> green [label=\"no\"];\n    refactor -> verify_green [label=\"stay\\ngreen\"];\n    verify_green -> next;\n    next -> red;\n}\n```\n\n### RED - Write Failing Test\n\nWrite one minimal test showing what should happen.\n\n<Good>\n```typescript\ntest('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {\n  let attempts = 0;\n  const operation = () => {\n    attempts++;\n    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');\n    return 'success';\n  };\n\n  const result = await retryOperation(operation);\n\n  expect(result).toBe('success');\n  expect(attempts).toBe(3);\n});\n```\nClear name, tests real behavior, one thing\n</Good>\n\n<Bad>\n```typescript\ntest('retry works', async () => {\n  const mock = jest.fn()\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\n    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())\n    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');\n  await retryOperation(mock);\n  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);\n});\n```\nVague name, tests mock not code\n</Bad>\n\n**Requirements:**\n- One behavior\n- Clear name\n- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)\n- Real product behavior is the target. Mocked behavior can never be the final deliverable or proof that the feature works.\n\n### Verify RED - Watch It Fail\n\n**MANDATORY. Never skip.**\n\n```bash\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\n```\n\nConfirm:\n- Test fails (not errors)\n- Failure message is expected\n- Fails because feature missing (not typos)\n\n**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.\n\n**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.\n\n### GREEN - Minimal Code\n\nWrite simplest code to pass the test.\n\n<Good>\n```typescript\nasync function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {\n  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {\n    try {\n      return await fn();\n    } catch (e) {\n      if (i === 2) throw e;\n    }\n  }\n  throw new Error('unreachable');\n}\n```\nJust enough to pass\n</Good>\n\n<Bad>\n```typescript\nasync function retryOperation<T>(\n  fn: () => Promise<T>,\n  options?: {\n    maxRetries?: number;\n    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';\n    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;\n  }\n): Promise<T> {\n  // YAGNI\n}\n```\nOver-engineered\n</Bad>\n\nDon't add features, refactor other code, or \"improve\" beyond the test.\n\n### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass\n\n**MANDATORY.**\n\n```bash\nnpm test path/to/test.test.ts\n```\n\nConfirm:\n- Test passes\n- Other tests still pass\n- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)\n\n**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.\n\n**Other tests fail?** Fix now.\n\n### REFACTOR - Clean Up\n\nAfter green only:\n- Remove duplication\n- Improve names\n- Extract helpers\n\nKeep tests green. Don't add behavior.\n\n### Repeat\n\nNext failing test for next feature.\n\n## Good Tests\n\n| Quality | Good | Bad |\n|---------|------|-----|\n| **Minimal** | One thing. \"and\" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |\n| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |\n| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |\n\n## Why Order Matters\n\n**\"I'll write tests after to verify it works\"**\n\nTests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:\n- Might test wrong thing\n- Might test implementation, not behavior\n- Might miss edge cases you forgot\n- You never saw it catch the bug\n\nTest-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.\n\n**\"I already manually tested all the edge cases\"**\n\nManual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:\n- No record of what you tested\n- Can't re-run when code changes\n- Easy to forget cases under pressure\n- \"It worked when I tried it\" ≠ comprehensive\n\nAutomated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.\n\n**\"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful\"**\n\nSunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:\n- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)\n- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)\n\nThe \"waste\" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.\n\n**\"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting\"**\n\nTDD IS pragmatic:\n- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)\n- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)\n- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)\n- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)\n\n\"Pragmatic\" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.\n\n"

    "text": "# Model Selection Must Never Cross Families\n\n**Date:** 2026-07-27\n**Context:** OmniHarness Claude worker launches, `resolveClaudeSessionModel`, ACP `session/set_config_option`.\n**Symptom:** Run `594224099b56` was launched as `claude-fable-5`, and both `runs.preferred_worker_model` and `workers.effective_launch_model` recorded it as such. Its transcript shows **301 assistant turns on `claude-opus-4-8`** — a different model family, for the entire session, with no warning anywhere.\n\n**Root Cause:** The resolver's last resort was `bestStandardContextOption(options)` — \"anything that runs without usage credits\" — with no family constraint. The adapter offered Fable only as `claude-fable-5[1m]`; the 1M filter emptied the Fable candidate pool, and the fallback landed on `default`, which was Opus 4.8. Three defects compounded:\n\n- **Context size outranked model identity.** Avoiding `[1m]` was allowed to change *which model ran*. The user asked for a model, not a context size.\n- **The 1M test read the wrong field.** `isOneMillionContextModel` inspected only `option.value`; the adapter's own recommendation is `{ value: \"default\", description: \"Opus 4.8 with 1M context\" }`, so the single largest 1M option in the list was classified as standard-context and became the \"safe\" fallback.\n- **`keep` was silent, and then the row lied.** `unavailable` threw and `pin` emitted `worker.model_pinned`, but `keep` emitted nothing and left `pinnedModel` null — so `effectiveModel: pinnedModel ?? requestedModel` wrote the *requested* model into the worker row as though it had run.\n\n**Fix:** One rule dominates: never leave the requested family — Opus, Sonnet, Haiku and Fable are different products, not fallbacks for one another. A family that is not offered at all is now the only refusal (`worker.model.family_unavailable`). Inside the family the resolver takes the requested **version** in whichever context size the adapter has it, and only drops to a lower version when that version is absent; context size is a tiebreak *between listings of the same model* and can no longer change which model runs. `isOneMillionContextOption` reads value, name and description. `keep` carries the resolved value and emits `worker.model_kept`, and `effectiveModel` is read back from the session's own config so a worker row can only ever record a model the adapter confirmed — but *only* the config the adapter actually handed back. `session/set_config_option` may acknowledge without echoing `configOptions`; reading the pre-pin snapshot back then reports the model the session was moved **off**, and because that snapshot is non-null no `??` fallback catches it. The read-back is gated on a refresh having happened, and a pin that throws records the surviving current value rather than the one it failed to set. With nothing requested, a 1M session moves only to the same model's standard-context listing — never to another model.\n\n**Verification:** `./node_modules/.bin/vitest run` (316 files, 2054 passed). `tests/lib/claude-session-model.test.ts` pins the real option list run `594224099b56` was offered and asserts it now resolves to `claude-fable-5[1m]`; `tests/server/agent-runtime/claude-model-pin.test.ts` covers the same through a live ACP handshake against a fake adapter. `tsc --noEmit` and `eslint` clean.\n\n**Prevention:** When resolving a request onto a provider's offer list, rank the constraints by what the caller can observe. Identity (which model) is not negotiable; incidental attributes (context window, alias spelling) are. A relaxation step that can silently change a non-negotiable attribute is a bug however sensible its own motivation — here, \"avoid usage-credit failures\" was a real goal that quietly rewrote the user's model choice. And whatever a resolver settles on, the durable record must be read back from the thing that will actually run, never from the request: a launch that records its own intent will keep insisting it was right.\n\n**Skill/Doc Updates:** None needed; this is the model-selection case of the existing control-plane invariant that persisted state must reflect confirmed reality rather than requested intent.\n"

ONLY THEN: Make the claim\n\nSkip any step = lying, not verifying\n```\n\n## Product-Surface Verification\n\nWhen the work involves an app, UI, or product surface, verification must cover more than whether a single requested feature works.\n\nKeep verification proportional. optimistic UI, caches, polling, streams, background jobs, or persisted runtime state,\n- persistence behavior for settings, preferences, drafts, and other user-managed state matches the approved decisions emit the planned named events, and a headless/scriptable check can assert the event sequence without relying on UI snapshots,\n- real errors are surfaced rather than silently swallowed or or obvious loss of confidence,\n- when the scope includes a frontend/backend boundary, frontend-visible failures preserve the real error details and stack traces expected by the approved design,\n- A family that is not offered at all is now the only refusal (`worker.model.family_unavailable`). Inside the family the resolver takes the requested **version** in whichever context size the adapter has it, and only drops to a lower version when that version is absent; context size is a tiebreak *between listings of the same model* and can no longer change which model runs. `isOneMillionContextOption` reads value, name and description. `keep` carries the resolved value and emits `worker.model_kept`, and `effectiveModel` is read back from the session's own config so a worker row can only ever record a model the adapter confirmed — but *only* the config the adapter actually handed back. `session/set_config_option` may acknowledge without echoing `configOptions`; reading the pre-pin snapshot back then reports the model the session was moved **off**, and because that snapshot is non-null no `??` fallback catches it. The read-back is gated on a refresh having happened, and a pin that throws records the surviving current value rather than the one it failed to set. With nothing requested, a 1M session moves only to the same model's standard-context listing — never to another model.\n+**Fix:** One rule dominates: never leave the requested family — Opus, Sonnet, Haiku and Fable are different products, not fallbacks for one another. The first repair constrained menu resolution to a family and made durable records reflect the adapter's confirmed model.\n \n-The follow-up fix resolves family identity in order from the option value, then its name, then only the leading identity clause of its description. Comparative marketing copy after separators can no longer add another model family to an option.\n+The 2026-08-02 repair removed menu resolution from explicit model selection entirely. OmniHarness passes the exact requested id, such as `claude-opus-5`, to the Claude process as `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` before startup. Claude's reported current model must then equal that exact string. A missing report or any mismatch stops the launch visibly; no family fallback, lower-version substitution, alias translation, or menu ranking is allowed. The menu resolver remains only for sessions with no explicit model, and its defensive path now also refuses unavailable versions and ignores comparative marketing copy when identifying options.\n@@\n-**Prevention:** When resolving a request onto a provider's offer list, rank the constraints by what the caller can observe. Identity (which model) is not negotiable; incidental attributes (context window, alias spelling) are. Never derive identity from unbounded prose: descriptions often compare products and therefore contain other family names. A relaxation step that can silently change a non-negotiable attribute is a bug however sensible its own motivation — here, \"avoid usage-credit failures\" was a real goal that quietly rewrote the user's model choice. And whatever a resolver settles on, the durable record must be read back from the thing that will actually run, never from the request: a launch that records its own intent will keep insisting it was right.\n+**Prevention:** Explicit model selection is an exact-value contract, not a recommendation.     "type": "input_text",
    "text": "# Lifecycle Observability & Resilience Testing\n\n> What we keep getting wrong, why our tests don't catch it, and the discipline that fixes it.\n\nRelated: `docs/architecture/hot-path-responsiveness-and-resource-leaks.md`\ndocuments the May 2026 reload/worker-streaming latency incident and the\nresource-ownership rules for keeping page bootstrap, SSE, and worker stream\npaths responsive while agents are running.\n\n## Multi-runner client lifecycle\n\nEach saved runner profile owns one `RunnerConnection` state machine and at most\none main event stream. A registry starts every profile connection, not only the\nvisible one. Switching the visible workspace changes active managers/query\ncaches and terminal ownership without closing inactive main streams.\n\nEvery bootstrap, snapshot, frame, retry, timer, and mutation checks profile and\nlearned runner identity before applying state. Stored cursors include the\nrunner's stream epoch. `runner.stopping`, `auth.session_revoked`, and\n`stream.resync_required` are typed terminal/control outcomes, not generic\nnetwork failures.\n\nElectron, VS Code, and Capacitor host bridges have bounded stream delivery and\nmust cancel upstream work on overflow. Mobile suspension persists cursors,\ncloses streams, and reconnects on resume; it must not claim background\ndelivery. Platform lifecycle contract tests live under `tests/electron`,\n`tests/vscode`, `tests/mobile`, and `tests/runtime-api`; real two-runner and\neight-runner journeys live under `tests/e2e`.\n\n## Interactive protocol invariant\n\nAn advertised interactive agent capability is operational only when the complete user journey is implemented: receive the request, append it to the unified worker stream, render an actionable control in the main conversation, submit the exact protocol response, and append a terminal outcome before resolving the agent request. Side-panel-only controls do not satisfy this invariant. Every form shape and permission option emitted by a supported adapter must be covered by a finite wire-to-UI regression matrix.\n\nRelated: `docs/architecture/timing-determinism-audit.md` records the May 20,\n2026 audit of race-prone frontend and control-plane patterns: cached snapshots\npretending to be authoritative, stale async callbacks, timer-owned actions,\ntimestamp-only ordering, and silent wake/lease contention.\n\n## Why this document exists\n\nOver a single afternoon we hit three production-class bugs that the existing test\nsuite did not catch and could not have caught:\n\n1. **Session fails to reconnect after a server restart and gives up after the\n   first attempt.** No user-visible message, no telemetry event, no recovery\n   incident — just a silently dead session.\n2. **`DELETE /conversations/:id` fails with a foreign-key constraint** because\n   related rows in dependent tables were not cleared first. The error surfaces\n   as an opaque 500.\n3. **Running plan-improvement agents fails because leftover state blocks the\n   new run.** The block is silent; the user sees nothing happen and assumes the\n   button is broken.\n\nThese are not unrelated bugs. They share a single root cause:\n\n> **The server makes state transitions that nobody observes.** Neither the user,\n> nor the UI, nor any test client can tell what the server decided. So bugs in\n> the *decision* (gave up too early, took the wrong branch, refused silently)\n> are invisible.\n\nThis document records what we learned and the rules we now follow so that this\nclass of bug stops shipping.\n\nRelated incident note: `docs/architecture/supervisor-worker-switching-incident.md`\nrecords the worker-switching failure from session `690d2fa9f2a7`, where\n`awaiting_user` was treated as runnable, Gemini workers were live but persisted\nas `starting`, and duplicate continuation workers were spawned.\n\nRelated direct-control note:\n`docs/architecture/direct-control-session-regressions.md` records the\n`ffb912d4d5d7`, `937e642f3535`, and `734cc38f4d7f` regressions around\nlifecycle noise, stale queued send-now state, missing unified-stream worker\noutput, and permanent \"Thinking...\" indicators.\n\nRelated state-staleness note:\n`docs/architecture/state-staleness-and-session-lifecycle-lessons.md` records\nthe `0785684884fa`, `14260d2a2df0`, `ecea142f7344`, and `18fc406457f3`\nregressions around stale SSE/cache payloads, queued-message races, direct-run\nstatus classification, unread markers, and worker-stream loading.\n\n---\n\n## What we found in the audit\n\nA targeted audit of `src/app/api/events/route.ts` plus the planning, recovery,\nand bridge-client subsystems revealed the structural gaps.\n\n### 1. The SSE stream is a snapshot stream, not an event stream\n\n`/api/events` emits exactly one named event: `update`, whose payload is the\n*entire* current state of the world for the selected run (messages, plans,\nruns, workers, planItems, clarifications, executionEvents, supervisor\ninterventions, queued messages, recovery incidents, review runs/rounds/findings).\n\nThere are no other named events. An observer cannot ask \"did a worker spawn?\"\nor \"was a recovery attempted?\" — only \"is the state now different?\" To answer\nthe first kind of question the client must **diff snapshots**, which is:\n\n- **Ambiguous** — many transitions produce identical visible state (a worker\n  that was reattached and a worker that was recreated both end up as\n  `status=\"running\"`).\n- **Lossy** — fast transitions can be coalesced inside a single snapshot\n  interval and disappear entirely. (e.g. `starting → running → completed`\n  inside one 15s window.)\n- **Forced to re-derive server decisions** — the client has to reconstruct\n  *why* state changed, which requires duplicating server logic.\n\n### 2. There is no event ID and no resume\n\nThe SSE frames have no `id:` field. There is no `Last-Event-ID` handling on the\nserver. A client that disconnects and reconnects gets a fresh snapshot and has\n*no way to know* whether events fired during the gap. For chaos testing (where\nwe deliberately drop the connection) this is fatal — we cannot assert\n\"between t0 and t1 the server emitted [X, Y, Z]\" because the wire format does\nnot carry that information.\n\nThere is a `?snapshot=1` bootstrap endpoint, which is good. There is no\n\"give me the events I missed since id N\" endpoint, which is the gap.\n\n### 3. Several decisions are invisible to the wire\n\nConcrete state transitions that **the server makes** but **never tells anyone\nabout**:\n\n| Transition | Where it happens | Wire visibility |\n|---|---|---|\n| Worker spawned | `bridge-client/index.ts spawnAgent` | None — inferred from a row appearing |\n| Worker reattached vs recreated after restart | `restart-control.ts` / recovery path | **None** — both look like `status=\"running\"` |\n| Recovery gave up after N attempts | `recoveryIncidents.autoAttemptCount` increments | Partial — count is visible but there is no terminal \"abandoned\" state |\n| Plan readiness reached | `derivePlanningStatus()` — runs **client-side** | **None** — it is a client-side derivation, not a server event |\n| Plan-improvement blocked by leftover state | `planning/review.ts` early-return | **None** — silent refusal |\n| Conversation delete FK violation | `/api/conversations/[id]` DELETE | None as a typed event — only a 500 response |\n| Message ack / persisted / streaming chunk | `conversations/send-message.ts` | Partial — only the resulting queued-message status |\n\nEvery row in this table is a bug class waiting to ship. If the server can\nsilently decide \"I gave up\", \"I refused\", \"I took branch B not A\", and the\ntest harness has no way to assert which branch it took, the test harness is\nstructurally incapable of catching the bug.\n\n### 4. The user-facing surface mirrors the test-facing surface\n\nThe reason \"leftover state blocked the run\" did not show a user message is the\n**same reason** no test could detect it: there was no event for it. Make the\nstate transitions observable, and both the UI fix and the test coverage\nfollow. Conversely, if a transition is observable only by re-deriving from a\nsnapshot diff, both the UI and tests will be brittle in the same ways.\n\nThis is the central insight: **observability for users and observability for\ntests are the same problem**.\n\n### 5. Playwright e2e is the wrong layer for resilience\n\nThe existing `tests/e2e/*.spec.ts` files boot Chromium. They are slow (tens of\nseconds per scenario), flaky against real subprocess restarts, and they\nexercise UI rendering rather than control-plane decisions. The bugs we are\nhitting are not UI bugs — they are control-plane bugs. We should be hitting\nHTTP/SSE directly, in Node, with no browser. The UI is one consumer of the\ncontrol plane; the chaos harness is another.\n\n---\n\n## The rules we now follow\n\nThese are not suggestions. They are the discipline that makes this class of\nbug stop happening.\n\n### Rule 1: every server-side state transition emits a named event\n\nIf the server makes a decision — spawn, reattach, recreate, give up, refuse,\ndelete, fail — that decision is published on the event stream with a\n**named event type**, not just a state delta. Examples:\n\n- `worker.spawned`, `worker.status` (with `prev` and `next`), `worker.terminal`\n- `worker.reattached`, `worker.recreated`\n- `plan.ready`, `plan.review.started`, `plan.review.finished`,\n  `plan.review.blocked` (with a `reason`)\n- `recovery.opened`, `recovery.attempt`, `recovery.gave_up`, `recovery.resolved`\n- `conversation.deleted`, `conversation.delete_failed` (with FK details)\n- `error.surfaced` — the catch-all for anything the user should know about\n\n**Rule of thumb:** if a server method has an early-return, a try/catch that\nswallows, or a branch that depends on a state check, it emits an event.\n\"Silent\" is a code smell.\n\n### Rule 2: errors that affect the user are events, not just response codes\n\nA 500 with a body is not enough. A 200 that quietly did nothing is worse. Every\nuser-relevant failure publishes `error.surfaced` with a stable code, a\nhuman-readable message, and the relevant run/worker/conversation ids. The UI's\njob is to render `error.surfaced` events into toasts/banners. The test\nharness's job is to assert that the expected `error.surfaced` event fired.\n\nA failure that does not produce an `error.surfaced` event is a bug — even if\nthe underlying behaviour is technically correct — because it is invisible to\nthe user and to the tests.\n\nThe event carries the stable id of the subject that failed. Conversation and\nworker failures use `runId`, `conversationId`, or `workerId`; account-only\nsettings failures use `accountId` rather than pretending an account is a\nconversation.\n\n### Rule 3: the event stream is SSE-spec compliant\n\n- Every frame has an `id:` field. IDs are monotonic.\n- The server keeps a bounded **ring buffer** (≥ 500 entries) of recent events.\n- The server honours `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect: it replays everything after\n  that id from the buffer, then resumes live streaming.\n- If the requested id has fallen out of the buffer, the server emits a\n  `stream.resync_required` event so the client knows to re-bootstrap from\n  `?snapshot=1` rather than silently miss events.\n\nThis is the SSE spec. We were not following it. We are now.\n\n### Rule 4: named events alongside, not instead of, snapshots\n\nThe existing `update` snapshot event stays. The UI keeps consuming it. The new\nnamed events are *additional* frames on the same stream. Clients that don't\ncare about a given event type ignore it. There is no `?test=1` flag, no\nseparate test endpoint, no parallel surface that can drift.\n\nIf a transition is worth emitting for tests, it is worth emitting in\nproduction. Anything else creates a second observability surface that will\ndiverge from reality.\n\n### Rule 5: chaos testing belongs in the client, not the server\n\nWe do **not** add fault-injection code paths to the server. We do not add a\n\"random failure\" mode. The server stays clean. Chaos lives in the test\nclient as middleware:\n\n- An SSE wrapper that can drop the connection on command.\n- A `fetch` wrapper that can fail a configurable percentage of requests.\n- A harness that can SIGKILL the spawned server process and restart it.\n\nFaults are seeded for reproducibility. Every failure has a seed; replaying\nthe seed reproduces the failure.\n\n### Rule 6: tests assert on event sequences, not on rendered state\n\nA scenario test reads like a transcript:\n\n```\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.spawned\", { runId });\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.status\", { next: \"running\" });\nchaos.killServer();\nchaos.restartServer();\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.reattached\", { runId });\n// not \"worker.recreated\", not absence — explicitly reattached\n```\n\n### Rule 7: cleanup waits for server-owned background work\n\nLifecycle scenarios may call routes that intentionally return before a direct\nworker turn finishes. That is fine for product latency, but it is not fine for\ntest cleanup to delete `OMNIHARNESS_ROOT` while those server-owned tasks are\nstill writing worker JSONL, recovery rows, or named events.\n\nRequired shape:\n\n- Fire-and-forget direct/planning turns are registered as background\n"
  }
]

    "text": "{\n  \"hasProduct\": true,\n  \"product\": \"# Product\\n\\n## Register\\n\\nproduct\\n\\n## Users\\n\\nSoftware developers and technical leads supervising several coding agents across local, remote, desktop, editor, and mobile surfaces. They work in long-running implementation and debugging sessions where clear state, rapid switching, durable recovery, and trustworthy control matter more than decorative presentation.\\n\\n## Product Purpose\\n\\nOmniHarness is a durable control plane for starting, observing, steering, and recovering ACP-backed coding-agent work. Success means a user can understand what every runner and worker is doing, take the next safe action quickly, move between devices and servers without losing context, and trust that failures, credentials, and recovery states are represented honestly.\\n\\n## Brand Personality\\n\\nCalm, capable, direct. The interface should feel like a precise professional tool with a human voice: dense when the work demands it, quiet when it does not, and explicit about uncertainty or failure.\\n\\n## Anti-references\\n\\n- Generic analytics dashboards built from interchangeable metric cards.\\n- Sci-fi command centers with neon decoration, fake telemetry, or gratuitous motion.\\n- Chat interfaces that hide execution state and recovery controls behind conversational chrome.\\n- Consumer onboarding that stretches a simple connection task into a promotional sequence.\\n- Interfaces that make remote, offline, authentication, or identity failures look like temporary loading.\\n\\n## Design Principles\\n\\n1. Show authority and scope. Every action, status, notification, and cache belongs visibly to one runner and one conversation.\\n2. Keep supervision fast. Frequent actions remain close to the active work, with familiar controls and strong keyboard behavior.\\n3. Make failure honest and recoverable. Name the affected runner, explain the state, and offer the smallest safe next action.\\n4. Preserve context across time and surfaces. Switching, reconnecting, and returning later should not erase drafts, cursors, or the user’s mental model.\\n5. Let the work dominate. Navigation and status remain legible but visually restrained around agent output, terminal content, and decisions.\\n\\n## Accessibility & Inclusion\\n\\nTarget WCAG 2.2 AA. All flows must support keyboard navigation, visible focus, screen readers, zoom and narrow layouts, live language changes, reduced motion, and status communication that does not rely on color alone.\\n\",\n  \"productPath\": \"PRODUCT.md\",\n  \"hasDesign\": false,\n  \"design\": null,\n  \"designPath\": null,\n  \"migrated\": false\n}\n"

The test is: would a user fluent in the category's best tools (Linear, Figma, Notion, Raycast, Stripe come to mind) sit down and trust this interface, or pause at every subtly-off component?\n\nProduct UI's failure mode isn't flatness, it's strangeness without purpose: over-decorated buttons, mismatched form controls, gratuitous motion, display fonts where labels should be, invented affordances for standard tasks. The bar is earned familiarity. The tool should disappear into the task.\n\n## Typography\n\n- **System fonts are legitimate.** `-apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, \"Segoe UI\", system-ui, sans-serif` gives you native feel on every platform. Inter is the common cross-platform default for a reason.\n- **One family is often right.** Product UIs don't need display/body pairing. A well-tuned sans carries headings, buttons, labels, body, data.\n- **Fixed rem scale, not fluid.** Clamp-sized headings don't serve product UI. Users view at consistent DPI, and a fluid h1 that shrinks in a sidebar looks worse, not better.\n- **Tighter scale ratio.** 1.125–1.2 between steps is typical. More type elements here than on brand surfaces; exaggerated contrast creates noise.\n- **Line length still applies for prose** (65–75ch). Data and compact UI can run denser — tables at 120ch+ are fine.\n\n## Color\n\nProduct defaults to Restrained. A single surface can earn Committed — a dashboard where one category color carries a report, an onboarding flow with a drenched welcome screen — but Restrained is the floor.\n\n- State-rich semantic vocabulary: hover, focus, active, disabled, selected, loading, error, warning, success, info. Standardize these.\n- Accent color used for primary actions, current selection, and state indicators only — not decoration.\n- A second neutral layer for sidebars, toolbars, and panels (slightly cooler or warmer than the content surface).\n\n## Layout\n\n- Predictable grids. Consistency IS an affordance — users navigate faster when the structure is expected.\n- Familiar patterns are features. Standard navigation (top bar, side nav), breadcrumbs, tabs, and form layouts have established user expectations. Don't reinvent for flavor.\n- Responsive behavior is structural (collapse sidebar, responsive table, breakpoint-driven columns), not fluid typography.\n\n## Components\n\nEvery interactive component has: default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error. Don't ship with half of these.\n\n- Skeleton states for loading, not spinners in the middle of content.\n- Empty states that teach the interface, not \"nothing here.\"\n- Consistent affordances across the surface. Same button shape. Same form-control vocabulary. Same icon style.\n\n## Motion\n\n- 150–250 ms on most transitions. Users are in flow — don't make them wait for choreography.\n- Motion conveys state, not decoration. State change, feedback, loading, reveal — nothing else.\n- No orchestrated page-load sequences. Product loads into a task; users don't want to watch it load.\n\n## Product bans (on top of the shared absolute bans)\n\n- Decorative motion that doesn't convey state.\n- Inconsistent component vocabulary across screens. If the \"save\" button looks different in two places, one is wrong.\n- Display fonts in UI labels, buttons, data.\n- Reinventing standard affordances for flavor (custom scrollbars, weird form controls, non-standard modals).\n- Heavy color or full-saturation accents on inactive states.\n\n## Product permissions\n\nProduct can afford things brand surfaces can't.\n\n- System fonts and familiar sans defaults (Inter, SF Pro, system-ui stacks).\n- Standard navigation patterns: top bar + side nav, breadcrumbs, tabs, command palettes.\n- Density. Tables with many rows, panels with many labels, dense information when users need it.\n- Consistency over surprise. ONLY THEN: Make the claim\n\nSkip any step = lying, not verifying\n```\n\n## Product-Surface Verification\n\nWhen the work involves an app, UI, or product surface, verification must cover more than whether a single requested feature works.\n\nKeep verification proportional. or obvious loss of confidence,\n- when the scope includes a frontend/backend boundary, frontend-visible failures preserve the real error details and stack traces expected by the approved design,\n-
